title: The crane and the crab
hookLine: a crane promises fish a better lake and eats them, until the crab (Jataka 38)

cards: It's the hot season, and the pond is shrinking. The fish can feel the walls of mud closing in. On the bank, a crane stands very still, looking sad on their behalf.
He's been worrying about them, he says. He knows a big lake not far off, deep, cool, full of lotuses, and he'd be glad to carry them there, one at a time. Free of charge.
In the Baka Jataka, the fish have an answer ready.

teach.b: First, the doubt. The fish tell the crane plainly: we've never heard of a crane who cared about fish. You want to eat us.

So the crane offers proof: send one of you to see the lake. They pick a big fish, blind in one eye, and the crane really does carry him there, lets him swim, and brings him back. It's real, the fish tells everyone.
Second, the trap. Now the fish line up, and one at a time the crane carries each off, but not to the lake. He flies to a tree beside it, pins the fish in a fork of the branches, and eats it.

teach.h: A TREE, A PILE OF BONES.
teach.b: The pile of bones under the tree grows. Third, the crab. At last only a crab is left.
The crane offers him the same trip.
Yes, says the crab, but I'd better hold your neck with my claws so I don't fall.
On the way, the crab sees the tree and the bones, and the crane says it out loud: I'm going to eat you too. Fourth, the grip.
The crab squeezes. Take me to the water, he says, or I'll take your head. The choking crane sets him down at the lake's edge, and the crab snips through his neck anyway.
A tree spirit who watched it all, the bodhisatta in this tale, speaks a verse: guile doesn't profit the guileful; look what the crane got from the crab. The crab never trusted the offer. He held on.

how: Buddhist teachers use the tale of the crane and the crab as a warning that deceit can turn back on the deceiver.

o: a fish blind in one eye
a crane or heron, a wading bird
a crab that lives in the shallows

games.q: the crane and the crab: tap the pairs.
p: promised a cool lake full of lotuses
sent first, and brought back to vouch
held on to the crane's neck

s: the fish trusted the crane right away
they said no crane ever cared for fish, so he carried one there and back as proof.
the crane really showed one fish the lake
that true trip is what made the trap work.
the crab let go of the crane once it was safe
he held on, and snipped through the crane's neck at the water's edge.

games.q: you're the last creature in a drying pond. a crane who has carried off every fish offers to carry you to a lovely lake. what do you do?
o: go. the others must be happy there.
go, but hold the crane's neck in your claws.
stay in the mud and hope for rain.
games.why: the crab goes, but keeps hold of the crane's neck. when he sees the bones, he squeezes, and the trickster is caught.

practice: Pick one offer in your life that sounds wonderful: a deal, a message, a person saying they'll take care of everything.

Ask the fishes' question, does this kind of helper usually care about me, and then the crab's, where's my grip if it turns out wrong? No need to decide anything; just hold both questions gently and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Baka. Crane or heron: the bird whose sweet offer ate every fish, until a crab kept hold of its neck. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali baka: crane or heron. the tale's name, Baka Jataka, comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: the crab remembers. A sweet offer can still have bones under its tree. Day eight hundred twenty-four.
